I'm giving it a thumbs up because I think it is worth the money overall, but I'm really on the fence about that decision. I describe some major issues below.

I'm a 30 year old working professional without a ton of time to to throw at games. While I've played this game for ~260 hours, it is pretty much my most played game (close second to Mount and Blade Warband from several years ago). I don't have thousands of hours to play games like other Steam users do. Thus, I value the quality of my overall gaming experience more, and generally stick to SP experiences because of the unpredictible time available to play games.

That being said, 7 Days to Die is an odd gem. It is a decent mix of open-world survival, sandbox, and horror. The game takes itself fairly serious as a survival game. In default settings, materials are scarce and upon death, there are semi-permanent penalties to the character's health and stamina. 

But the game is maybe too clunky and unsupported by the devs to take itself that seriously. This is unfortunate because the game obviously has a lot of potential. Imagine playing Minecraft in survival mode (I use Minecraft as an example, but this can apply to any open world game), where every 5-30 minutes, a Creeper randomly spawns right next to you and blows you up. This can happen when you are down in a cave, when you are a 20 minute walk from your base, etc. In some instances you survive with a shred of health remaining, but it kills you much of the time and there's just nothing you can do. As someone who takes the survival aspect seriously (as does the game itself), this would be really offputting. Playing on permadeath or Iron Man mode (which I do in other games) just isn't a real option unless you have infinite patience for that sort of thing.

So how does that apply to 7 Days to Die. Well, when you go into a house, there are often zombies sleeping in corners or on the floor that you want to sneak around or carefully and quickly try to kill. Fighting zombies in close quarters is not easy in this game. So you take out the 3-6 zombies in a house and start to go through it for loot. Suddenly, as you are opening a drawer, a you get hit from behind from a zombie. You are stunned, meaning that you turn and move very slowly. By the time you turn around and get 1-2 hits in, the zombie has already killed you. You drop all your stuff, spawn 15-30 minutes away, and your stamina and health are reduced by 10%. This happens constantly, not because you missed a zombie, but because there is some ongoing bug where houses randomly 'reset', causing all the zombies you killed to suddenly reappear, sometime right next to you when you're facing the other way.

Sometimes you can survive these instances, but often it's unavoidable. Either way it's really frustrating and a downer. The game has a lot of replayability, so I go back to it every once and a while. But then I run into one of these situations, sit there staring at the screen for a few seconds, and typically just power down the game. "But it is in alpha and should be fixed, right?" You can't make that assumption with this game. Some things the devs fix or improve, and other things get ignored for years.

What I can tell you is that in the most recent 15 minute preview for alpha 17 (which will come out 1 to 6 months from now, who knows really..), the lead developer was doing a walkthrough to demonstrate some new additions. The dev mentioned they haven't played the game in over a year (like on survival mode I guess?), and this happened to them 2-3 times when they were fighting zombies in a basement. The dev seemed fairly oblivious to the bug. So, as of a few weeks ago, this bug that has been in the game for over a year still hasn't been fixed.

The dev video was pretty damning honestly. I've never seen a lead dev so unfamiliar with their own game before. He went up to a boar (one of 4-5 animals in the game), attacked it, and was surprised when it fought back and killed him. This is really strange. My guess is the guy cashed out on this game and hired a few other people to develop the game on his behalf and he just kind of chimes in every once in a while. They don't seem to be making a ton of progress, as the last update was over a year ago. If that this the case, what can we really expect for future updates? I'll leave that question for you to answer.

In a nutshell 7D2D is what early access games should be. It has a good range of features to keep you entertained while updates come out. The devs were friendly and helped me with a FoV problem I had with the game (I suffer from acute simulation sickness).

What put me off is seeing people and curators endorse the game as “like minecraft”

[b]Can we please get out of this trench of comparing everything to Minecraft?
The genre is Voxel world not “Minecraft”, it’s like calling all FPS games “Like CoD”.[/b]

There is much I still have to explore and it honestly is one of the best survival games I have ever played. Compared to a game such as DayZ everyone seems rather friendly. Which is much better than other zombie world based games like Dayz (not making many comparisons, for obvious reasons) because not many people seem to shoot me on sight. Which was refreshing.

Once you get access to guns everyone loves you (totally unrelated I’m sure). 
Definitely worth a pickup. I can’t find much wrong with it. The only problems are purely cosmetic and don't break the game. Which is nice because every build seems to be very stable, aside from the few bugs that do get fixed rapidly.

The only major complaint I have is that the range of melee weapons and a zombie’s reach feels misleading, if a reticule turned green when in range and red when out of melee range I would be happy with this. Aside from that, completely worth the money - nice to see someone finally did the genre justice.

7 Days To Die, a long trip from 2013 until now.
I saw this game being played on youtube and didn't expect a lot, but seeing the constant updates every month on my feed grew my hopes along the time.

Something I have to point out in my own perspective (and perhaps many) in horror games is, as soon the player is given a weapon, the horror factor either decreases a LOT or goes away entirely.
NOT in this game!

If you play It with headphones at night, alone (no other players), I guarantee this game will scare you even if you have a weapon while exploring for resources. 
The very rare moments of music in this game is eerie, the ambient sounds (majorly in the "Burned Forest" and "Wasteland" biomes) and the silence always put you on edge, and when a random horde spawns close to you and those "battle music" drums start rolling, you start looking everywhere for your safety.

Exploring the ruins can be scary too, mostly if you enter a room, and right next to the door out of your vision is a zombie right on your face, gurgling right into your ears and puching you, It will be a guaranteed jumpscare.

And when you are done and/or your inventory is full, you race back to your base and as soon you enter the "claimed" area, nothing beats hearing that piano indicating you are back to your home and safety, but the melody gives out a vibe that you're not out of the woods yet, and any moment a horde decides to spawn with 3 "screamers" ready to spawn in even more zombies. (No joke, those screamers are terrifying at any part of the day!)

The Blood Moons, a huge experience farming event, which can also be the end of your base if you REALLY aren't prepared. If you decide to fight this event in your base, good luck and always be on the watch, the hordes don't come from the same direction.
But once you beat It and the clock shows 4AM, hearing that sweet piano tune indicating the night is over and a new day dawns, and the event is over, the relieve is real.

Graphics.
The zombies are really well made and give the look of a real threat, even more if they are irradiated ones cause those are a pain to deal with, and don't get me started on the screamers!
Another huge upgrade to the game is the "cosmetic" debris.
I still remember WAY BACK in the day, where construction vehicles were designed and made with separate blocks, making it weird destroying them for resources. Now they are It's own models, allowing the player to break them completely.

Gameplay also got a huge change too before.
You unlocked recipes by reaching new levels and unlock specific perks and such.
Now, you have to look for magazines about the topic (like weapons, materials, workshops, etc...), and THAT WAS HUGE, It makes the player explore more and more and that is wise. It keep people enganged.
It was before, but now It's even more.

The hitbox of the zombies is also superb. If they move a lot, the hitbox moves along, and if in the last 0.5 second, they move their head and you shoot, It's a miss. Making It a crucial decision in dealing with groups. Go for a quick kill with a gun and probably miss, or go melee and risk getting overwhelmed?

Exploring great difficulty ruins is challeging in terms of navigation and fighting your way in, but the rewards are really good.

If you want a good and fun survival experience, play It with friends.
If you prefer a horror game, play It like I said in the start of this review: alone, headphones, at night.

I've been with this game since its early Early Access days, and that's exactly why this review hurts to write.

The biggest problem is that the game has gradually abandoned what made it unique in the first place.

The new skill progression system based on finding and reading books makes absolutely no sense. Instead of learning through experience, practice, or survival, your character becomes stronger because they happened to find the correct piece of literature. It feels artificial, gamey, and completely disconnected from the world.

At the same time, traders have become the center of the entire gameplay loop. Sure, giving them quests sounds useful on paper, but now you're constantly running errands just to unlock progression. Survival, resource management, inventory decisions, and the feeling of struggling through a hostile post-apocalyptic wasteland have all been pushed into the background.

What used to be a survival sandbox now feels like a chain of mandatory tasks.

One of the things I loved most about the older versions was the freedom. You could go almost anywhere from the beginning. Some areas were more dangerous, some required better equipment or preparation, but the world was open to you. The game trusted you to make your own decisions.

Now entire portions of content are locked behind masks, reputation requirements, unlock chains, and quest progression. Instead of exploring because you're curious, you're exploring because the game has finally granted you permission.

The result is a much more restrictive and arcade-like experience.

Every update seems to add another layer of artificial progression while removing the sense of freedom, danger, and discovery that originally made the game special.

Maybe new players won't notice the difference. But after 782 hours, having watched the game evolve from its earliest versions, I can honestly say that I find it less engaging, less immersive, and significantly less enjoyable than it used to be.

I used to lose myself in this world for hundreds of hours.

Now it mostly feels like doing chores.

Fun game. Building mechanics are still being worked on. Weapons feel good. Melee is a lot better than it used to be, and still being improved. After over 1k hours in this game, I still enjoy it, though I have the following comments:

1. The dev team really seem to hate it when you figure out how to beat their zombie AI, which seems to be based off the mind of a civil engineer.

2. The gyrocopter is not a good addition in my opinion. It detracts from the "being on  the road" adventure you get from all other vehicles. This may be different on larger maps which may justify it I guess.

3. Some talents are underpowered, and some are borderline game breakingly powerful. But this is a work in progress, so expect nerf/buffs in future.

I'm going to expand upon the AI for a moment. As of Alpha 20, the game uses AI that was intended for bandit npcs for the zombies, and, if I'm being honest, it's a bit of a problem. It makes certain base designs fundamentally unworkable during a blood moon. Without going into too many details, zombies should not be smart enough to spot and exploit weak points in a given structure. As far as i've seen from videos and my own experiences. it means that everyone sort of converges on a very similar design that exploits the AI, which kinda sucks. I would have preferred when AI was dumber and you could build a load of interesting designs just for fun. But, once again it's a work in progress.

Itemisation is weird in the game. Every major increment, there seems to be an arbitrary item in the game that is non-craftable, and relatively rare, and becomes your bottleneck for almost all activities, forcing you to invest talent points into "lucky looter" and "better barter". As of Alpha 20, this is acid, which is used for making chem stations and tyres, and forms a hard gate into vehicles. You WILL get the perks for creating vehicles long before you acquire enough acid to build a motorbike. This effectively means minibikes (which used to be a staple of the game) are useless, as by the time you have enough acid to make tyres, you can already make motorcycles, and so can skip the minibike.

This is just an example of the type of arbitrary item gating that goes on in the game. It used to be wrenches , then the minibike book, then it was glass beakers, now it's acid. 

By mid game, most early game activities become redundant. If you don't take farming perks early game, there is no point taking them later, as you will be flooded with food. 

The mid-late game is mainly mining, looting, trader missions, and repairing your blood moon base and making ammo. 

All these issues are of a balance nature, however, and as such, are subject to change, and whilst they can be a pain, it still does not change that this game is genuinely fun, challenging, and an overall excellent time sink.

Okay. How to review this game. As you can see, I have a lot of time into this game. I'm so very torn on how to review this game because my opinion of it is bittersweet, to put it bluntly. 

First, the good. 
-7 Days to Die is probably the best survival/scavenging game made, to date. 
-The world is pretty enough to make you want to explore more. 
-The POI's are unique enough to want to investigate. 
-The loot is great, everything in the game has a use, and the progression is decent. 
Obviously with nearly 1,900 hours invested in this game, over it's lifetime, it's a good game with lots of replay value. This game has the most value of any game I've ever owned, and honestly, that in and of itself is huge. 

Now, for the bad, because as of late, I've been very very disenchanted with the development, and methods for developing the game. (Mind you, some of these gripes can be adjusted with settings,) but frankly, from where the game started, all the way to where it's gone over the past couple of years, they are very much valid, and quite honestly worth addressing here. 

-The development of the game is what I could only describe as "Vindictive" and "petty." What I mean by this, is that no matter what you do, no matter how much you progress, you cannot ever be considered "Safe." Any time the community finds a way to make a base type, "Safe" the developers change the entire AI so that these methods no longer work. The issue with this is, at the end of the day, there is no point at all in progressing, as the zombies rip through just about anything that you'd build, in a matter of minutes, and the defenses are easily dispatched and insanely underwhelming. Back in the day, I used to work my butt off to get to concrete and steel, so I could make a defensible base. It gave me a reason to play and something to work towards. And because of this gripe, I can no longer play this game without getting bored after a week or so, and quitting for months. This is what killed the game for me, overall. 

-The leveling system. Before the game's leveling system was changed, you used to be able to skill up by preforming the tasks that you wanted to level. This was amazing, and was very much like "real life." This was one of the things that drew me to the game in the first place. How do you get better at something? Practice! Now basically, you kill zombies, gain XP and spend points from level-ups. Frankly, it makes no sense, and this change was explained away in the most stupid way possible, and it made me lose a LOT of respect for the development of this game. In fact, this is when/why I stopped playing the game as much as I used to, and was the start of my distaste for it. Apparently "leveling by doing" isn't "realistic," and in order to conform to the desires of what I call the "Immersion Turd" community, they've effectively done away with one of the main things that made the game unique and overall enjoyable/rewarding to play. 

-Map Size. I understand the need to cap the size of the map for performance reasons. Unfortunately, with the introduction of vehicles, it cuts the size of the map down, immensely. Finding borders and endless oceans as a border is a complete Buzz-kill, as the game itself isn't rewarding to a nomadic player, which this game eventually forces you to be, the longer you play. Simply put, the maps, even random-gen, is capped, and small, even at the maximum map size. 

-Leveling Speed. I'm not going into this very heavy, but when you need to increase the XP gain to 300% in order to pace the game at a normal speed.... There's a problem. 

-This is a mild gripe, and barely worth putting here, but it is something to note. TFP have seriously lofty goals with their updates. This is fine, but at the same time, it's not. Because of this, updates can take 6 months at minimum, to release. Most take nearly a year. Which is fine... I guess, as most of their major updates change the game greatly. The fact of the matter is, the development has been ongoing for far too long, it's far too slow, and frankly, this is one of the many many things that are destroying the game's long-term success.

-Finally, this one speaks for itself by this point.... There is NOTHING in the way of endgame. There's no reason to even get there, and by the time you're at a point where you can hold your own, you're so beaten down and burned out from the issues listed above, that it only leaves a bad taste in your mouth. This has been the issue with this game since day one.

So. For the majority of people, I would completely recommend the game. Obviously I got my money's worth. The game is fine. I will still say that this is probably the best survival game to date. It's worth buying. But if the devs don't stop intentionally screwing over their community, and ignoring the need for endgame content, they're going to destroy one of the best games of the decade. I'm on the fence on whether I would recommend this game to a friend, I really am. But to the average player, the game is fine. For those who started playing this in the beginning? It's a shadow of what it once was, and it's painfully obvious that the potential that it had was, (putting it mildly,) squandered. It's for this reason why I cannot effectively say whether or not I'd recommend it. Try it out for yourself, it's worth that much alone. ;)

I have almost 950 hours into this game. I sort of think of it as a Minecraft for grown ups, although I have played well over 950 hours in that game too, lol

I enjoy most the scavenging and base building aspects in this game. Sometimes I play with the zombies turned on, other times I just hone my skills and tool around surviving. It's a plus to be able to control that. I can get lost in the game easily. I know it has been in Alpha a long time, but I still enjoy it and seem to never get tired of it. I think I started playing it around Alpha 16, now Alpha 18 is about to drop.

I was concerned about transitioning from A16 to A17, but I quickly got back in the groove after a DayZRP break. I'm hoping A18 will be almost like getting a new game with all the changes I've seen coming. Plus the 7 Days community create mods that can greatly enhance your gameplay, so that you play it the way you want to. Modding the game is also fairly easy using .xml mods. You can't find them here in the Workshop I think, but at the TFP's official forums and The Nexus Mods website for sure. They're free and generally well done.

The game does have its problems. I have a pretty bad@ss computer and still can only play on 1920x1080 resolution with no lag or stutters. I'm hoping optimization is better in A18. The game is nice looking though even at that lower resolution. Learning how to survive, what skills to gain, and how to build bases to protect you are all fairly easy to gain some mastery in. Reading guides, watching YouTube video play throughs and trial and error will eventually get you where you want to be as a survivor.

The zombies can be set to run or always walk. Mine always walk when I play with them on, because it makes more sense to me. They are dead and decaying after all :P I don't want to play 28 Days later style, so I don't. That's one of the things I like, you can play with longer nights, longer days in between hordes and air drops everyday. Or you can make it hard as he!! with zombies always running, horde nights every night, loot taking longer to respawn and air drops only once a week. You can even control how fast or slow you progress with leveling and skill acquisition. That is one of the great things about the game. It also has a creative mode to let you just go in and experiment with skills and crafting until you feel comfortable enough to add zombies to the mix.  I've played both coop and single player. I enjoy both modes, but most of my time has been on single player. 

The game challenges me, is great fun for me, and as I said, I can play for hours when I have the time. If you like crafting, survival and zombies, this game is a great addition to your game library. I've never regretted getting it, even if it is still in Alpha.

I've been playing since alpha 8, the good, the bad, the slow, the fast. It's the single game that has held my interest through all the years. 3100 hours and counting. A18 is awesome, and what's on the roadmap is going to end in a great game. Easy mod-ability has given it lasting power after the 'new' wears off. And it's just plain fun to play!

📢HISTORICAL HISTORY

BEFORE 1.0:
In 2022 during the development of 7d2d one of the original developers, who had been with TFP since the start left the team due to a lawsuit over unpaid royalties which resulted in the loss of his valuable vision, coding skills, ideas, and many assets that were removed from the game since his departure.

To complicate matters not long after a tragic event unfolded when another developer tragically passed away in a car accident. This accident significantly impeded map progression and various other areas of the game as it meant losing his insights, guidance, and advancements of the projects he had been working on before his death.

After the significant losses of both developers, TFP hired numerous graphic art designers to implement their ideas and influences, rather than focusing on long-standing issues and bugs that have persisted over the years. 

Unfortunately it seems, most of the new art personnel seem to prioritize their vision of what the game should be which would include many unnecessary twitch commands and changes while removing core assests that where in the game for many years such as clothing and jars. 

Over the last couple years it seems TFP have really lost focus on what 7d2d is first, a survival game.
To compound the current issue there is only seems to be one developer who appears to be dedicated solely to fixing longstanding bugs. This individual is not able to soley focus on bug fixs due to him being overwhelmed with work on bandits for 3.0 release, resulting in many current bugs not being resolved in a timely manner leading to the persistence of the bugs from one alpha version to the next.

Furthermore, during the whole time 7d2d has been around we must also take into account the two brothers who over the years have consistently shown differing visions for the game's future, plans, and roadmaps. 
The brothers who are the founders of 7d2d have been involved in every phase and aspect of the game since its conception they created during a holiday dinner that they envisioned many years ago.
Over the years the reason we see different elements, assests and features in one alpha version compared to another is due to the on going addition and removal of features and items, the brothers have had distinct ideas and viewpoints regarding the game's direction from one alpha to the next in which they want to proceed. Resulting in many different systems being implemented and taken out over the years.

Moreover, players are continually urging for the 3.0 bandit update, which I believe has diverted their focus away from more pressing matters allowing significant bugs to persist. It is not a question of the developers lacking personnel to develop the game, as they have hired people the last couple years.
The challenge lies in that these new hires often have different objectives and do not focus on bug fixs and most of them where not present from the beginning. 
This is where effective leadership is crucial to align everyone towards a common goal and ensure a unified focus. Instead of continuing with the current 3.0 road map i believe the game would benefit more in the long run if TFP would designate their time and resources to a bug patch. The player community would appreciate bugs fixed alot more than a few features added.

AFTER 1.0:
recently since 1.0 released i have seen a major shift in prioritys and bug fixs from TFP and have noticed improved work on fixn bugs.
Over the years, PvP would be fortunate to receive just one fix which sometimes took a couple of years to implement.
Since the release of version 2.0, PvP has experienced more fixes in this brief period of time than in all of history prior to that combined.
With all the NEW fixes it sends a clear message to PvP players who participated in this game over the years that TFP have shifted their focus to support PvP.
This is exhilarating, if not exciting, for those who play PvP.

7 Days to Die — Roadmap: Promise → Reality → Current Status​
7 Days to Die — Roadmap: Promise → Reality → Current Status​
1) 2021–2022 — Bandits were already a stated development target. In November 2021, the official forum discussion referred to bandits as coming with A21. By July 2022, the A21 development diary specifically listed active work on “Bandit AI and animations.” So bandits were a concrete development target well before the 1.0 roadmap.

2) April–July 2024 — TFP publishes the formal post-1.0 roadmap. Version 1.0 was scheduled and ultimately released July 25, 2024. The published roadmap then laid out three post-1.0 stages: Storm's Brewing — Q4 2024, with weather/biome progression, wardrobe, crossplay and console RWG; A New Threat — Q2 2025, with bandits, UI/main-menu overhaul, event system and a new quest type; and The Road Ahead — Q4 2025, with trader overhaul, story mode, Steam Workshop support and another new quest type.

3) 2025 — The original dates slip. Storm's Brewing did not arrive in Q4 2024. Its V2.0 development diary acknowledged that development had taken significantly longer than anticipated and ultimately targeted stable for June 30, 2025. Importantly, that same official-forum roadmap still listed V3.0 A New Threat: Bandits + UI + Event System + New Quest, followed by V4.0 The Road Ahead: Trader overhaul + Story + Workshop + New Quest.

4) Late 2025–early 2026 — More intermediate updates appear. V2.5 Survival Revival shipped December 8, 2025, followed by V2.6 stable on April 1, 2026. By this point the simple 1.0 → 2.0 → 3.0 → 4.0 roadmap had evolved into a more fragmented release structure.

5) February–March 2026 — The version numbering and roadmap are reorganized. The sandbox-focused update originally discussed under the 2.x line became V3.0, eventually named Dead Hot Summer; its own dev diary notes that it had previously been referred to as Sandbox Siege. Official-forum clarification at the time said that what had originally been the bandit update was effectively being shifted to V4.0, while features previously bundled together would receive separate numbered updates later.

6) March 24, 2026 — Behaviour Interactive acquires The Fun Pimps. This is more precise than saying only 7DTD was sold: Behaviour announced its acquisition of The Fun Pimps. Behaviour stated that TFP would continue leading development and creative leadership would remain unchanged, while Behaviour would add resources, expertise and production capacity to accelerate the existing roadmap. On the same day, TFP programmer faatal stated that 3.0 and 4.0 were both currently in development, with 5.0 and 6.0 planned out.

7) June–July 2026 — V3 actually ships. Dead Hot Summer V3.0 introduced the large sandbox-option system, magnitude/item changes, POI/signage work and other systems; experimental went live June 15. V3.0.1 was stable by July 13. Then V3.1 Henpocalypse went stable July 27 on PC, PlayStation and Xbox.

8) August 19, 2026 — Where the roadmap actually stands today. The clearest public future direction remains V4.0 / the Threat or bandit update. At the time of the Behaviour acquisition, the official forum said bandit work was proceeding and that 4.0 would focus on bandits; faatal confirmed 4.0 was already in development. However, 5.0 and 6.0 have only been publicly described as “planned out.” I cannot find a newer detailed TFP/Behaviour roadmap assigning dates and feature lists to them. The old Road Ahead items—story, trader overhaul, Steam Workshop support—and the old A New Threat items such as the event system/new quest type are therefore not currently attached to a verified public release date in the way they were in the 2024 roadmap.

Clean current roadmap​
✅ 1.0 — Released
✅ V2.0 Storm's Brewing — Released
✅ V2.5 / V2.6 — Released
✅ V3.0 Dead Hot Summer — Released
✅ V3.1 Henpocalypse — Released
🔄 V4.0 — Bandit / Threat update — publicly established direction; no firm public release date I can verify
⏳ V5.0 — internally planned; public feature/date roadmap not published
